# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Zach Cregger's "I was naive" comment and the way we talk about fidelity in adaptations

**Score:** 133
**Body:** Zach Cregger recently said that he had been "naive" about the reaction to his Resident Evil. He seems to have assumed that fans of the games, being fans like himself, would be interested in a survival-horror movie set in Raccoon City even if it wasn't another retelling of Leon, Claire or Jill's story. The trailers suggest that assumption was wrong. A lot of film fans liked what they saw, while a noticeable part of the game audience reacted to the changed chronology, characters and events by saying that this simply wasn't the Resident Evil adaptation they had wanted.

I haven't seen the film, so I'm not trying to judge whether Cregger's Resident Evil is good. I'm more interested in the language around the disagreement. In a lot of Anglophone film discussion, asking whether an adaptation is faithful to its source is treated as a fairly unsophisticated fan concern. The implication is often that people asking for fidelity simply want to see something they already know, while changing the source demonstrates interpretation, authorship or imagination.

I don't find that opposition very useful. Fidelity is obviously neither necessary nor sufficient for a good adaptation. Kubrick's The Shining is an easy example of the first point, while plenty of excellent close adaptations settle the second. But it doesn't follow that fidelity has no aesthetic value. Part of the problem is that we use "fidelity" to describe several different things and then talk about them as though they were the same.

# There is more than one kind of fidelity

The limits of literal fidelity are easiest to see with novels. Interior monologue, tense, free indirect discourse and hundreds of pages of narrative obviously cannot just be moved into a two-hour film unchanged. But being faithful does not have to mean reproducing every scene or every line.

The Lord of the Rings is usually described as a faithful adaptation even though it rewrites Faramir, expands Arwen and removes the Scouring of the Shire. Villeneuve's Dune films also make substantial changes to structure and character, especially Chani, but are still widely regarded as serious attempts to engage with Herbert's work. When people call these adaptations faithful, they are clearly talking about something other than literal correspondence.

One kind of fidelity is what I would call surface fidelity: keeping plot events, dialogue, visual designs, chronology and characters relatively close to the source. Another is interpretive fidelity: trying to preserve a defensible understanding of what the source considers important. That might include its tone, moral emphasis, character relationships, central conflicts or the role particular characters play in the work.

I don't think a work has one objective "essence" that can be recovered perfectly. People can disagree radically about what Watchmen, Dune or The Shining means, and interpretive fidelity is still an interpretation. But that doesn't make the idea useless. We already argue all the time that some readings of a work are better supported than others.

This also explains why an adaptation can reproduce costumes, dialogue and even individual images very closely and still be accused of missing the point. Snyder's Watchmen is probably the most obvious example. Whatever your opinion of the film, the usual criticism is not that it failed to reproduce enough of the comic visually. The criticism is that faithfully reproducing the images did not necessarily reproduce the comic's attitude toward those images. The opposite can happen too. An adaptation can change events quite dramatically while still being seen as preserving something more important about the source.

Games introduce another possibility, which I think is especially relevant to Cregger: experiential fidelity. Cregger is trying to reproduce aspects of the experience of playing Resident Evil. You begin relatively powerless, worry about ammunition, find better weapons over time and move through a hostile environment while your resources diminish. He is changing characters and continuity while trying to preserve the survival-horror rhythm of the games.

Some fans are asking for something else. They want fidelity to Raccoon City's established history, characters and chronology. So both sides are actually making claims about fidelity. They disagree about what the film should be faithful to. That seems closer to the actual disagreement than saying that the fans want fidelity while the filmmaker wants freedom.

# Why this matters more in the IP era

Auteurism gave film criticism good reasons to take the adapter's interpretation seriously. A director should be allowed to make a film rather than act as a photocopier. The situation gets more complicated, though, when the source itself has an audience much larger than the audience of the filmmaker adapting it.

That audience doesn't own the work and shouldn't have veto power over artistic decisions. But it includes people who have spent years thinking about what the work is, how its parts relate to each other and why particular elements matter. Calling all of that "fan entitlement" doesn't explain much.

Recent game adaptations make the issue fairly obvious. HBO's The Last of Us preserves many major story beats while deliberately changing others, with Neil Druckmann directly involved. Fallout tells an original story but stays inside the history, institutions and logic of Bethesda's world. Arcane expands and reconstructs material from League of Legends, with Riot deeply involved in deciding how those characters and that world could develop.

These are very different adaptations, and none is a transcription. What they have in common is a close relationship between the adaptation and the authority behind the source. Creator or rights-holder involvement obviously doesn't guarantee a good result, but these examples make it hard to argue that greater distance from the source automatically means greater creativity.

# The awkward Resident Evil counterexample

There is an obvious counterexample inside the same franchise. Paul W. S. Anderson's six Resident Evil films departed enormously from the games and were commercially successful. If box office were the only test, there wouldn't be much more to say.

But commercial success and success as an adaptation are not necessarily the same thing. Anderson's films developed their own audience and their own continuity, while many game players continued to see them as something quite separate from the games. Cregger himself has said that he never watched the earlier movies because they didn't look like the Resident Evil he loved.

I find that comment interesting because it is very close to what some skeptical fans are now saying about his film. Cregger could look at the Anderson films and think, "That isn't the Resident Evil I care about." Most people would consider that a perfectly understandable judgement about the relationship between an adaptation and its source. Cregger himself has also said that he understands why some fans are disappointed by what they have seen of his version.

The wider discussion is where the asymmetry appears. When a filmmaker says that an adaptation did not preserve what mattered to him about a source, we tend to understand that as an interpretation of the work. When fans say that a change removes something that mattered to them about the source, the judgement is much more likely to be described as purism, nostalgia or entitlement.

Fans can be wrong, of course. They can misread a work, confuse personal attachment with artistic necessity or obsess over trivial details. Directors and screenwriters can misread works too. So I don't understand why the adapter's reading of the source is so readily discussed as interpretation while the audience's reading is so often discussed as attachment. That is the part of this debate that interests me most.

# Why Japan makes an interesting comparison

The question of who gets to make a legitimate claim about what matters in a source is also why I think Japan is useful as a comparison. I don't mean that Japanese adaptations are simply more faithful, and Japan clearly doesn't have one unified philosophy of adaptation. Miyazaki's Howl's Moving Castle alone would make that difficult to argue.

What is interesting is that in large parts of the manga, anime and game industries, the judgement of the original creator, publisher or rights-holder is given a more visible institutional role. Publisher involvement, production committees and the common use of kanshu, or supervision by the creator, publisher or rights-holder, make source-side authority much more explicit.

The controversy over the television adaptation of Hinako Ashihara's manga Sexy Tanaka-san is a useful example. Ashihara wanted important parts of the drama to remain faithful to the manga and expected to be able to revise material when that wasn't the case. During production, repeated revisions took place while the publisher and television production developed different understandings of how much alteration was acceptable and how the author's conditions had been communicated. Eventually Ashihara herself wrote the final two episodes, which was a highly unusual arrangement.

After the series aired, people involved in the production discussed the circumstances publicly on social media, and the dispute became a major controversy. Ashihara died in January 2024. I don't think it is responsible or necessary to reduce her death to a simple causal explanation. The relevant point here is what happened afterward. Nippon Television and Shogakukan both investigated the production process. Their reviews identified serious communication problems and differences in how the conditions of the adaptation had been understood, and both companies subsequently issued or revised guidelines concerning adaptations of existing works.

The discussion therefore went beyond whether the changes made the television drama better or worse. It also became a discussion about when an author should be informed of changes, how agreements with the author should be communicated to writers and production staff, how much weight should be given to elements the author considers essential, and what responsibilities come with adapting somebody else's work.

In that context, fidelity wasn't only an aesthetic preference. It was also an ethical and institutional question about the relationship between the source and the people adapting it.

There are Western equivalents, of course: copyright, moral rights, contractual control and authors publicly objecting to adaptations of their work. Japan hasn't somehow solved the problem, and I'm not suggesting its production system should be copied. The comparison matters for a simpler reason. It shows that asking for a source to be preserved does not have to be understood only as nostalgia, fear of change or artistic conservatism. It can also be a claim about authorship, responsibility, interpretation and the limits of what an adapter has been entrusted to do.

If the legitimacy given to source-side judgements depends partly on cultural and institutional convention, then dismissing fan demands for fidelity may also be a convention rather than the inevitable result of a more sophisticated view of film.

# What I actually want to discuss

I don't think faithful adaptations are inherently better than loose ones. Fidelity is one legitimate creative goal among others, and deviation is not automatically more creative than preservation. A film can preserve the plot and lose the theme. It can preserve the theme while changing most of the plot. A game adaptation can change both while trying to reproduce the player's experience. An adaptation can reject all of these and still be a great film.

So "faithful or free?" isn't really the question I'm interested in. Nor am I especially interested in whether critics literally believe fidelity is bad. Most people will say, "Of course not, it depends on the film," and I agree.

What interests me is what happens when audiences actually ask for fidelity.

1. If a filmmaker can say, "This is what really matters in the source," change the work accordingly and have that treated as a legitimate interpretation, why isn't a fan saying, "This change removes something essential from the source," treated as an interpretation too?
2. If fidelity itself isn't considered a negative value, but people who ask for it are routinely described as purists, nostalgic or entitled, aren't we just moving the negative judgement from the preference to the person expressing it?
3. If radical deviation from a source is a legitimate aesthetic preference, why isn't wanting an adaptation to preserve its characters, world, themes or narrative structure just as legitimate?
4. With Cregger's Resident Evil, where exactly is the line? Cregger could decide that Anderson's films did not resemble the Resident Evil he loved. If a game fan makes essentially the same judgement about Cregger's film, at what point does that stop being an interpretation of the source and become "fan entitlement"?

That seems to me like a more interesting question than simply asking whether adaptations should be faithful.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. We’ve been circling this idea a lot with The Odyssey too and I think the answer I’ve reached is a bit circular but I don’t really see any other way to engage with this irresolvable dilemma: If the film is good, then its adaptation choices are well founded.

And “it’s different” is not a persuasive, interesting or meaningful critique.

Does the film work? That’s the question, always will be.
2. The important thing is that the movie is good and consistent regardless of faithfulness. Rosemary's Baby is a great adaptation that is on one extreme of this spectrum, while Starship Troopers, Re-Animator, The Shining or Apocalypse Now are examples on different points of said spectrum.


However, I am surprised by Cregger's own surprise to fan negativity to departures from source elements, considering that the one big common fan complaint about all of the previous Resident Evil adaptations was that they weren't faithful in relation to the chronology and characters. I don't know why he was expecting them to react in an opposite way to this. The bemoaning was to be expected. It is only once the movie is out that an overwhelmingly positive viewership reaction can change this.
3. I love video games and I love Resident Evil but I really have no sympathy for the haters, who I would say largely don't understand film as an artform and just want the novelty of seeing something they're familiar with recreated in live action. I have even less sympathy for them when you consider that they already tried that with Welcome to Raccoon City and everyone still got mad about it.

A lot of the arguments, I'm not even sure what they want. The most common complaint is "this looks like a zombie film with a few Resident Evil references", but Cregger has stated multiple times that the film's structure follows that of an RE game, where the character moves from environment to environment, collecting weapons and managing ammo, while encountering different threats, and that if the movie was a game called Resident Evil 10, no-one would question it.

But it's not canon, as adaptations almost never are, and so a few minor creative liberties have been made, specifically setting it in the modern day and in the winter, as is his right as the director who wants to make the best film possible.
  - It's like how every 'fancast' is just a game of finding the working actor who looks the most like a character in a photo. No thought to acting ability, demeanor, tone, etc. Or that make up, prosthetics and an entire costuming department are a thing. There's no imagination in these people. I don't know how anyone can be a Resident Evil fan and not be excited, or at least curious, about the best new horror director in the business - an evident RE fan - taking this on. 

As you said, they seem to just want the jangling keys moments of seeing exactly what they've already seen, recreated beat for beat in live action. How boring. Or simply have diminished the argument to better reflect the natural state of the average gamer: to whine.
    - I have similar feelings towards gamers’ reservations towards Elden Ring. Threads just full of Jack Black jokes, and having no idea who’s helming the project.
  - I saw the trailer, with the protagonist scrounging for bullets in an old house, taking the empty shotgun off the mantle, rummaging around in a chest next to a desk with a typewriter. It seems like window dressing, but the idea of picking up seemingly disparate items and scrounging for weaponry is pretty intrinsic to the classic Resident Evil experience, and it’s clear that Cregger understood that on a pretty deep level - otherwise, why build a trailer around it?

All I can do is look at the haters and shake my head. This is why we can’t have nice things. 
    - To me as a fan, this reaction by other fans is really odd in general because one of the most praised RE games in the last decade is RE7 and it has almost nothing to do with the OG characters and plot. It also doesn’t even completely fit the gameplay as it’s a first person shooter as opposed to third person or fixed camera. 

I’m hoping once the movie releases properly it will be more accepted, but right now besides wanting a beat for beat live action nostalgia trip, this film seems pretty readily acceptable as a Resident Evil film and I’m looking forward to it 
4. I think the comparison between adapting novels and adapting games breaks down in an important way actually.

I’m not biased. I play video games and I love film. I’ve played resident evil and yet I’ll watch and most likely enjoy this film and I think the discourse from fanbases is often overblown and unnecessary.

A video game is already an audiovisual narrative medium. When you adapt a novel, you are translating between fundamentally different forms of storytelling. Interior monologue, prose, narration, and hundreds of pages of character development have to be converted into images, performances, dialogue and editing. Changes are therefore inevitable.

Resident Evil, in this case, does not present that same problem to the same degree. 
The games already give you the characters, the environments, the monsters, the visual language, the pacing, the set pieces, and importantly, the experience of moving through the world. A filmmaker is not being asked to figure out how to translate a literary device into cinema. They are adapting something that already speaks in many of cinema’s own languages. This is important and makes the question of fidelity somewhat different.

There is obviously still room for interpretation. A two hour film cannot reproduce a 15 to 20 hour game literally, just as The Lord of the Rings could not reproduce Tolkien literally. But I think there is a meaningful distinction between condensing an existing story and reconstructing it into a fundamentally different story that merely uses its experiential mechanics.

If I watch an adaptation of The Lord of the Rings, I understand why the Scouring of the Shire has to go or why Bombadil was omitted. If I watch Dune, I understand why characters, chronology and internal monologue have to be reorganized. Those changes are being made because cinema has different structural requirements.

But if a Resident Evil film changes the established characters, history, locations and chronology while arguing that it is preserving the “experience” of Resident Evil, I think fans are justified in asking “why do those particular changes have to happen?”.. Because the experience of Resident Evil isn’t completely separable from the world in which that experience takes place.

You don’t experience Resident Evil as an abstract survival horror machine. You experience it as Jill, Leon or one of the other established characters. You experience the Spencer Mansion, the police station, the streets of Raccoon City, and all the accumulated mythology surrounding them. The mechanics create the experience, but the fiction gives those mechanics meaning.
And this is where I think the comparison to novels becomes particularly limited. 
Most people encountering a film adaptation of a novel can encounter the film without having previously inhabited that world. The film can function as their primary introduction to it. If they love it, they may then go to the books and discover another, deeper version of the story.

Harry Potter is, to me, an obvious example. The films introduced millions of people to the world, while the books existed and released as an additional layer of depth. The relationship between the two works could therefore be somewhat asymmetrical: the film could stand on its own as a cinematic experience, while the novel remained the larger textual world behind it.

Video games are different because the audience has often already spent an enormous amount of time inhabiting the source world before the adaptation ever exists. A player can spend hundreds of hours within a game. They don’t simply read about a character. They control them. They walk through their environments. They hear their voice. They learn the geography of their world. 
The audience therefore isn’t just familiar with the source material. They have lived inside it. 

That, in my opinion, creates a different psychological relationship between source and adaptation.

When a novelist describes a character’s childhood in three paragraphs, the reader may imagine that character however they want. But when a player has spent dozens of hours controlling Leon Kennedy, watching his mannerisms, hearing his voice and moving him through Raccoon City, Leon isn’t merely a literary construct anymore. He has become an audiovisual and experiential memory connected to the source material.

Likewise, Raccoon City isn’t just a setting described in text. Players have already formed a mental map of it. The police station isn’t merely “a police station.” It is a particular place that they have navigated, memorized and emotionally associated with danger, discovery and progression. So when an adaptation changes those things, it isn’t merely changing details. It can collide directly with the audience’s existing experience of the work.

This is why I think “experiential fidelity” is useful but incomplete.

Yes, a filmmaker can preserve the survival horror rhythm of Resident Evil while changing the characters and continuity. But the question is whether the experience of Resident Evil can really be separated so cleanly from the fictional identity that gives that experience its emotional weight.

Imagine adapting The Shining while preserving only the experience of being trapped in an increasingly hostile environment, but replacing Jack, Wendy, Danny, the Overlook Hotel and the basic mythology with entirely new characters and locations. You could argue that the film preserves the “experience” of The Shining, but at some point the argument becomes so abstract that almost any psychological horror film could qualify.

That is the danger of reducing fidelity to mechanics or atmosphere.

If the only things that need to remain are “you are powerless, resources are scarce, the environment is hostile and tension gradually increases,” then the adaptation may be experientially faithful to survival horror without being particularly faithful to Resident Evil.

I think this is what some fans are reacting to. They aren’t necessarily demanding that every hallway, line of dialogue or gameplay sequence be reproduced one for one. They may instead be saying that there is a threshold at which interpretation stops being adaptation. That threshold is obviously subjective, but it is still worth discussing.

There is also a strange paradox here.. Games arguably give filmmakers more freedom than novels, while simultaneously giving them less permission to radically reinvent the source. More freedom because games often contain enormous amounts of gameplay, optional content, repetition, exploration and mechanical padding that can be compressed or discarded. Less permission because so much of the fictional world already exists in cinematic form.

Cregger can absolutely restructure Resident Evil. He can add characters, remove subplots, compress chronology, change the pacing and reinterpret themes.
But he doesn’t necessarily need to invent an entirely new framework to make the story cinematic. The games have already done much of that work.

This is also why I think the size and maturity of gaming as a medium matters. Video games are no longer a niche source material sitting underneath a film adaptation. They are the largest entertainment medium in the world, with enormous communities that have spent years or decades engaging with particular fictional universes.

Resident Evil isn’t simply a game that happens to have characters and lore that can be borrowed for a movie. It is an established transmedia identity an has been for decades. The audience’s investment therefore precedes the adaptation in a way that is somewhat different from the traditional relationship between a film and its literary source.

And that changes the burden placed on any filmmaker. The question shouldn’t simply be:“Can you make a good Resident Evil movie without reproducing the games?” Of course you can. The more interesting question is:“Why are you changing the things you are changing?”
That’s the same standard we apply to literary adaptations. Nobody should object to change merely because it is change. The important question is whether the change serves the new medium, the interpretation, or the story being told.

If Cregger changes something because the structure of the game would produce a terrible two hour film, that’s completely defensible. If he changes something because he has a genuinely interesting reinterpretation of a character or theme, that’s also defensible. But if established characters, history and world are discarded primarily so the film can tell an unrelated story while retaining the Resident Evil name and survival-horror mechanics, then calling the result “experientially faithful” doesn’t necessarily answer the criticism.
It may simply be defining fidelity so narrowly that the most important elements of the source have been excluded from consideration.

I don’t think fans are wrong for wanting interpretive, surface and experiential fidelity simultaneously. Those aren’t mutually exclusive. An adaptation can change the structure while preserving the characters. It can compress the chronology while preserving the mythology. It can create new scenes while retaining the established relationships. It can invent cinematic sequences while still making Raccoon City feel like Raccoon City.
In fact, the most exciting possibility is probably not choosing between fidelity and reinterpretation, but finding the places where the two can coexist. That’s what makes the best adaptations so satisfying. They make you feel that you are seeing something new while simultaneously recognizing the thing you loved. 

And perhaps that’s the real difference between a game adaptation and a novel adaptation.
With a novel, the filmmaker often is tasked with turning this story into a movie.With a game like Resident Evil, the filmmaker is tasked with making a movie out of something that already feels like a movie to a large group of people who already played it. That is a much more complicated adaptation problem.

Frankly, how much he humanizes these characters, to the point you in some case wish to spit in their faces for how nasty they are, is chilling... and of course just as much kudos to the incredible actors he collaborated with throughout his career. 

My favourites are Through a Glass Darkly, Winter Light, and a toss-up between Hour of the Wolf and Cries and Whispers. Yes, I've seen all the classics and loved them dearly, but these aforementioned ones stood out to \*me\* most for some reason or another. Through a Glass Darkly especially might be my favourite film ever. I was stunned watching it for the first time, frankly feeling called out, which I'd never felt by a film. Winter Light... big, difficult, questions I ongoing struggle with myself... and both Hour of the Wolf and Cries and Whispers... deep feelings of hate/detest, which I ashamedly harbour myself... I can be a real piece of shit. 

The only film of those which I saw which I didn't absolutely love was The Virgin Spring, though it was still great- Bergman can do no wrong. 

Although I didn't cite The Silence among my top-3, it's still way up there, and I very often recommend the faith "trilogy" (although I'm aware he later denounced referring to it as such, iirc).

Persona was a landmine I'm still trying to unpack and possibly maybe never will- will require multiple viewings!

## 4. Sirāt (2025): Ambiguous or Entirely Inscrutable/Uninterpretable?

**Score:** 23
**Body:** So, I ended up finally watching Sirāt this week as part of my university's film society. Anyway, my friend and I were quite mystified by the praise heaped upon it. It immediately seemed like a very cheap film (full of shock and sometimes impressive spectacle but lacking in true thematic cohesion). So, I did what I usually do whenever I see a film and wrote up some ramblings about it on my Letterboxd. I've posted my "review" (but it's really more of a log primarily for myself) below, because I haven't really seen many of the positive reviews address the potential issues I identified, and regardless, I'd be very curious to hear other people's perspectives on the film: 

"The Wages of Fear (Gaspar Noé Remix) 

I can't help but feel the acclaim for this film is because it is what feels like yet another calculatedly ambiguous film (where some ideas/themes are touched on but never developed into a thesis but the overall ambiguity of the piece allows critics/viewers to project onto it and thus elevate its meaning, which is a cheap way for artists to gain acclaim without ever risking a true thesis). 

Aside from the script being full of contrivances and absurdity in the last act (and very unearned and emotionally manipulative shocks that are just noisy spectacles, since the major one just serves to shock and offer "big emotion" with massive trauma rather than anything generative), the major issue here for me actually lies in something I'd usually praise: the lack of backstory or explicit characterisation as well as context. Whereas in other films we receive enough information about characters based on their actions, here the film is largely rendered unreadable to me because we simply don't understand these characters or how the central figure of the father changes (we know that he, like every character here, is a moron, but he seems quite loving and caring, so why has he taken his son to an unstable war zone, and is he trying to find his daughter because he has been a bad father in the past or because he is just extremely worried for her or because he thinks the world is ending and wishes to reconnect before time is up or because he is overly protective/fixated, and where is the mother? How long have they been searching for the daughter?). He's simply a non-entity that denies the themes any ability to develop. Also, are we meant to see the ravers as complete idiots or likeable dreamers (either way, I do appreciate the final act exposing the faux-transcendence they attempt to espouse)? There's a difference between nuanced characterisation and just unclear sketching. The vague military conflict creates similar problems: is this a regional conflict? Has this been going on for a long time? I like how its scope and causes are ambiguous, but since we never really get any sense about its nature, we are also denied the proper ability to justifiably draw any readings from how the characters respond or don't respond to it (the characters seem casual about it, but they are also ravers detached from reality, so is it that they are irresponsible or justified to be wary or tired of the soldiers?). Also, the film feels far too out of time (with very few of the contextual causes of such problematic or short-sighted behaviour being properly identified or explored, which seems pretty important for a film looking at human nature). The questions just go on and on...

Yes, the sound design and score/soundtrack are stunning (the most stripped-back techno that draws out both transcendent and chthonic qualities to it, the pulses being either like mantras of Buddhism or something malevolent), and there are undoubtedly some interesting ideas here, but none of them are ever explored in satisfying or comprehensive detail (they're usually introduced and then dropped, with each of the acts introducing rather distinct themes but never offering an interplay between them). Similarly, whilst there are some incredible images and moments of montage, especially towards the start (as well as a sometimes great understanding of editing techniques, such as that one slow dissolve of Luis into the dark landscape), there's also many superfluous shots and scenes as well as some very boringly blocked shots (where there isn't nearly as much being drawn out symbolically from a scene as there could be).

I left this feeling a bit miserable and frustrated (although I did laugh quite a bit from its mounting absurdity and slapdash construction). I've crawled through the durst, but aside from occasional moments of purely emotional, primal transcendence, what am I meant to be getting from this misery?"

What's more great is that how Na hong jin made this film so realistic, grounded, subtle, less theatrical, and it's more like a documentary with intense camera works. It works because sometimes it exaggerated things but most of the times it takes some time to progress the plot.

Our guy carries the movie like he's personally being charged rent for every frame. His performance is built around physicality. Jung-ho is constantly running, sweating, shouting, breathing heavily and falling. You can almost feel his Iungs burning. And that's essential because it doesn't makes him ultimately a strong player. When he escapes from police, you don't get to see he suddenly run so fast that nobody could catched him.

The most cherry on top moment was for me is where Na Hong-jin gets absolutely fucking evil as a filmmaker. The film gives you this innocent child. And you know what the adult world is doing around her. That's the contrast; Childhood innocence vs adult corruption. Police bureaucracy. Sex work, Violence, Murder. The kid doesn't understand the machinery surrounding her. The audience does.

That's painful to see.

This is important. At first you're basically screaming to the legal systems and police which i did the same is

"BRO JUST DO YOUR FUCKING JOB."

But the film is doing something deeper.

The police aren't simply incompetent because the screenplay needs them to be. They're trapped inside procedures, hierarchy, politics, bureaucracy and institutional self-preservation. The system is designed to process information.

But processing information isn't the same as saving someone.

That's the tragedy.

Finally, The camera doesn't constantly sit safely somewhere watching the action. It feels unstable and Handheld. Close. You're not observing the chase from a comfortable distance. You're inside the panic. That instability makes the scenes feel documentary-like.

When i mentioned the screenplay is tight. I really meant it. The screenplay keeps giving you just enough hope. Not enough to relax, Enough to believe,

"Maybe."

Then

NOPE.

If everything goes badly constantly, you stop caring. You need hope. The Chaser gives you hope and then crushes it. The ending is fucking devastating. And what makes it work isn't merely the event itself.

It's the accumulation.

Everything you've watched has been pushing toward that emotional collapse. The movie has spent two hours making you believe:

"Maybe this time."

And then it basically tells you:

No.

That's why it hurts.

In the end we see our guy Finally picking up the signature hammer of Serial killer to kill him but unfortunately he couldn't kill due to the interruption of police officer which just shows that in the end our guy lost against injustice.
Overall, I wanted to review every minute details cause i wanted. I loved this film because it was great at every aspect. Highly recommended, This will be my only last long reviews of film.
